lessons.title: The Core Four: The Fed, ECB, BOJ, and PBOC as Global Liquidity Creators

body.text: Four central banks, the Fed, the ECB, the BOJ and the PBOC, dominate global liquidity creation, but they do not matter equally for India. Their currency's reserve status, their balance sheet size, and how open their capital account is decide how directly each one's policy reaches the NSE and BSE.

children.text: The RBI runs its own monetary policy, but it is not one of the world's liquidity creators in the sense this course uses the term. Global liquidity is dominated by four central banks, sometimes called the "Core Four": the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, the Bank of Japan, and the People's Bank of China. What earns them that status is not just balance sheet size. It is a combination of three things: whether their currency is used to fund and settle cross-border trades and positions, how large their balance sheet is relative to the global economy, and how open their capital account is, meaning how freely money can move in and out of their currency.

Each central bank's balance sheet has moved since, so check the Fed's H.4.1 release, the ECB's weekly financial statement, the BOJ's balance sheet data, and PBOC disclosures directly for current numbers.

body.label: BOJ Balance Sheet vs GDP
body.context: The BOJ is the only one of the Core Four whose balance sheet has exceeded the size of its own country's annual GDP, a scale no other G4 central bank has approached.

children.text: Why the PBOC Is the Odd One Out

By sheer size, the PBOC's balance sheet would suggest it belongs alongside the Fed and ECB as a driver of global liquidity. In practice, China's capital controls mean the renminbi does not move freely across borders the way the dollar, euro or yen do. PBOC easing shows up in Chinese credit growth and, through trade and commodity demand, in economies like India that sell into or compete with China. It rarely shows up as a direct swing in FPI flows into the NSE or BSE the way a Fed rate decision does. The PBOC matters to India mostly through the real economy channel, not the liquidity channel.

body.title: Five Moments That Show Each Central Bank's Reach

events.title: Fed Launches QE1
events.description: In response to the Global Financial Crisis, the Fed begins large-scale asset purchases, effectively starting the modern era of central bank balance sheet expansion as a routine policy tool.

events.title: ECB's "Whatever It Takes" Moment
events.description: ECB President Mario Draghi pledges to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro, calming the eurozone sovereign debt crisis and paving the way for the ECB's own large-scale asset purchase programmes.

events.title: BOJ Launches Quantitative and Qualitative Easing
events.description: Under Governor Haruhiko Kuroda, the BOJ commits to aggressive asset purchases to fight two decades of deflation, eventually growing its balance sheet larger than Japan's entire GDP.

events.title: PBOC Devalues the Yuan
events.description: China's central bank allows a surprise yuan devaluation, triggering a global equity selloff, including a sharp fall on the Nifty, and showing that PBOC actions can transmit shocks despite capital controls.

events.title: The Yen Carry Trade Unwind
events.description: A BOJ rate hike and a strengthening yen force a rapid unwind of yen-funded carry trades worldwide. Global equities, including the Nifty, fall sharply even though the Fed had not changed policy that week, showing that liquidity shocks do not only originate at the Fed.

children.text: The Fed vs the BOJ: Two Very Different Funding Currencies

body.title: US Dollar vs Japanese Yen as Funding Currencies

columns.label: Fed / US Dollar
points: The world's primary reserve and funding currency, used to price and settle most global trade and cross-border debt
Historically higher policy rates than Japan draw carry trade money into the dollar
Fed balance sheet moves (QE, QT) directly drive global dollar liquidity conditions

columns.label: BOJ / Japanese Yen
points: Near-zero rates for decades made the yen the cheapest major currency to borrow in
Investors borrow cheap yen and invest in higher-yielding assets abroad, including EM equities and bonds, the classic "yen carry trade"
A BOJ rate hike or a strengthening yen can force a rapid, disorderly unwind, as seen in August 2024

body.title: A Shock With No Fed Fingerprints
body.scenario: In early August 2024, the Nifty fell sharply over a few trading sessions. The Fed had not announced any new rate decision or balance sheet action that week. Instead, the BOJ had raised its policy rate and the yen had strengthened rapidly against the dollar.
body.prompt: If a student in this course assumed every global liquidity shock traces back to the Fed, how would you correct that assumption using what you now know about the Core Four?
body.modelAnswer: The Fed is the single most important liquidity creator for India, but it is not the only one. The August 2024 episode was driven by the BOJ, not the Fed. Years of near-zero Japanese rates had funded a large "yen carry trade": investors borrowed cheap yen and used it to buy higher-yielding assets worldwide, including EM equities. When the BOJ raised rates and the yen strengthened, the trade became unprofitable and investors had to unwind it quickly, selling assets across markets, including in India, to repay yen borrowings. This shows that global liquidity shocks can originate at any of the Core Four, and that a purely Fed-centric mental model will miss shocks like this one until they have already hit the market.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: Why does PBOC policy transmit to India mostly through trade and commodity demand rather than through direct FPI flows, unlike the Fed?
options: Because China's economy is smaller than the US economy
Because the renminbi is not accepted for cross-border trade
Because China's capital controls limit how freely money can move in and out of the renminbi
Because the PBOC does not use a balance sheet
body.explanation: China's tight capital account controls mean the renminbi cannot move as freely across borders as the dollar, euro or yen. PBOC easing shows up in Chinese domestic credit and, through trade and commodity demand, in economies like India, rather than as a direct swing in FPI flows into the NSE or BSE.

points: The "Core Four" (Fed, ECB, BOJ, PBOC) dominate global liquidity creation because of their currencies' reserve or funding status, balance sheet size, and capital account openness.
The Fed matters most directly to India because the dollar prices and funds most cross-border trade and FPI positioning.
The BOJ matters through the yen carry trade: cheap yen borrowing funds risk assets worldwide, and a BOJ hike or a stronger yen can force a sudden global unwind, as in August 2024.
The PBOC's balance sheet is large, but capital controls mean it transmits to India mostly through trade and commodity demand, not direct liquidity flows.
Global liquidity shocks do not always originate at the Fed. Reading the cycle correctly means watching all four, not just one.
